Paramount's Street Fighter won the weekend at the domestic box office with $31 million. But nobody in the business is talking about the winner — they're talking about second place.

Because the movie in second place is a nearly three-hour, R-rated documentary that opened on just 855 screens — and it just made more than $15 million, the biggest box office opening for a documentary in more than 20 years.

That's the verified record. Now let's lay out what it is.

The film

You Can See Everything, from A24, is a genre-bending documentary by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim about disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes. Holmes was convicted of wire fraud and conspiracy to defraud Theranos investors, and she reported to federal prison in 2023.

The filmmakers spent roughly three years on the project in secret, filming Holmes and her partner, hotel heir Billy Evans, in the weeks before she went to prison — 34 days before she surrendered, to be exact. The film then premiered as a surprise secret screening at the Telluride Film Festival on September 6, before opening theatrically on October 16. Fielder granted zero pre-release interviews. The mysterious teaser became a meme in its own right — Seth Meyers and Kate McKinnon recreated its "why would I deceive you?" moment on Late Night last week.

The numbers

From those 855 theaters, the film pulled more than $15 million — updated figures put it at $15.6 million, or about $18,000 per theater. A24 reported more than 2,000 sold-out screenings by Sunday morning. The audience was young: 70% of opening-weekend moviegoers were under 35. Exit polling from PostTrak found 92% of viewers gave the film its highest "definite recommend" rating.

The comparisons are the kind a documentary almost never gets to make. It is the biggest non-music documentary opening since Michael Moore's Fahrenheit 9/11 in 2004, the biggest opening for any film on fewer than 1,000 screens since Borat in 2006, and A24 called it "one of the largest limited-release openings of the 21st century." Critics agree: the film holds a 99% fresh score on Rotten Tomatoes and a record-high 4.8 rating on Letterboxd.

The rest of the weekend

Street Fighter — one of the first releases from postmerger Skydance, created when Paramount merged with Warner Bros. Discovery earlier this month — took the top spot with a $31 million domestic debut from 3,575 theaters and a $51.1 million global opening, starring Andrew Koji, Noah Centineo and Callina Liang. Behind the documentary, Other Mommy took $8.4 million, Whalefall $8 million, and Sense and Sensibility $7.3 million. The domestic box office totaled about $101.6 million for the weekend, up roughly 45% from the comparable weekend last year, and year-to-date ticket sales stand near $8.2 billion — almost 20% ahead of 2025.

The take — analysis

Rentrak's Paul Dergarabedian said it best: "Sometimes the biggest story at the box office isn't necessarily the movie that finishes at No. 1." That's this weekend. Here's my read on why it happened, and it's three things.

First: scarcity. Five weeks of marketing after a secret premiere, a teaser that became a meme, and a young audience terrified of spoilers turned a documentary into a must-see event. Second: the Fielder factor. An internet-famous personality with a cult following treated like a blockbuster property — A24 marketed the man as much as the movie. Third: quality. You can manufacture urgency, but 2,000 sellouts and a 92% "definite recommend" don't happen for a film people aren't genuinely buzzing about after the credits roll.

The takeaway for the industry: the theatrical documentary is not dead. It was just waiting for someone to give it a theatrical reason to exist.
